# Extending the welfare decomposition from class

In class we studied a decomposition of the gain in utilitarian welfare from moving from a laissez-faire economy to one with perfect insurance (i.e. where everybody receives the same allocation). We also saw that the same decomposition works for a comparison between *any* two policy regimes, where neither necessarily provides perfect insurance. Today we'll apply it to a life-cycle model. First, let's restate the definitions from class in this setting.

## Setup and definitions

Let there be a unit measure of agents in the economy, indexed by $i\in[0,1]$. As before, assume that agents rank probabilistic sequences of consumption according to:

$$ V^{r}_{i} = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(c^{r}_{i,t})\right]$$

where $\{c^{r}_{i,t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}$ is the sequence of consumption that agent $i$ enjoys under regime $r\in\{A,B\}$. Utilitarian welfare is $W^{r} = \int V^{r}_{i}di$.

Let $\mathcal{V}(c)$ be the value of receiving consumption $c$ for sure in every period:
$$\mathcal{V}(c) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(c) = \frac{1-\beta^{T}}{1-\beta}u(c).$$
The *certainty equivalent* $\bar{c}^{r}_{i}$ solves $\mathcal{V}(\bar{c}^{r}_{i}) = V^{r}_{i}$ for $r\in\{A,B\}$, and the *average certainty equivalent* is
$$ \bar{C}^{r} = \int \bar{c}^{r}_{i}di.$$
Finally, let $C^{*}=\int y_{i,t}di = \int c_{i,t}di$ be average consumption in the economy. We assume that the resource constraint always holds and there is no aggregate uncertainty, so $C^*$ is the same in both regimes, and $\mathcal{V}(C^*)$ is the welfare that perfect insurance would deliver.

## The decomposition

Following the lecture, we split welfare in regime $r$ into the perfect-insurance benchmark minus two costs:
$$ W^{r} = \mathcal{V}(C^{*}) - \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(C^{*}) - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{r})\Big]}_{\text{cost of imperfect insurance}} - \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{r}) - W^{r}\Big]}_{\text{cost of unequal certainty equivalents}}$$

The first cost is the loss from risk: even if everyone received the *average* certainty equivalent, this is lower than average consumption because people face uninsured risk. The second cost is the loss from inequality: certainty equivalents differ across people, and with concave utility this unequal allocation is worth less than giving everyone $\bar{C}^{r}$.

Since $C^*$ is unchanged by the policies we consider, the welfare change when moving from regime $A$ to regime $B$ is:
$$ W^{B} - W^{A} = \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B}) - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\Big]}_{\text{insurance}} + \underbrace{\Big[\big(W^{B} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})\big) - \big(W^{A} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\big)\Big]}_{\text{redistribution}}$$

## Converting to consumption equivalents

These terms are in utils. As in class (and [recitation 2](../recitations/recitation-2.qmd)), we convert them into consumption equivalents. With CRRA utility, scaling consumption in every period by $(1+\omega)$ scales every value by $(1+\omega)^{1-\sigma}$. So the total consumption equivalent of moving from $A$ to $B$ is
$$ 1 + \omega = \left[\frac{W^{B}}{W^{A}}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)}.$$
We can split this multiplicatively as $1+\omega = (1+\omega_{I})(1+\omega_{R})$ by writing
$$\frac{W^{B}}{W^{A}} = \frac{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\times\frac{W^{B}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{W^{A}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}$$
which gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
1+\omega_{I} &= \left[\frac{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} = \frac{\bar{C}^{B}}{\bar{C}^{A}} \qquad &\text{(insurance)}\\
1 + \omega_{R} &= \left[\frac{W^{B}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{W^{A}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} \qquad &\text{(redistribution)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The $\omega_{I}$ term is the welfare effect of changes in insurance (how the average certainty equivalent changes). The $\omega_{R}$ term represents changes in the equality (or inequality) of the distribution of certainty equivalents.

# Adding taxes and transfers to the model

In recitation 2 we wrote down code to solve the life-cycle savings model. All of that code is saved in [`income_tools.jl`](https://github.com/josephmullins/ECON4538/blob/main/recitations/income_tools.jl), so we can load it in one line:

```{julia}
include("income_tools.jl")
```

Below we'll show how the code is extended to allow for a generic system of taxes and transfers. The only function that changes is `solve_value`. The version saved in `income_tools.jl` looks like this (the saved version also allows net income to depend on age, `net_income(y, t)`, which we will use in recitation 4):

```{julia}
#| eval: false
function solve_value(ai, yi, V, p, t)
    # note here we assume that p contains a *function*
    # called net_income (if it does not, net income = gross income)
    (;σ, β, Π, r, asset_grid, income_grid) = p
    net_income = get(p, :net_income, identity)
    a = asset_grid[ai]
    y = exp(income_grid[yi, t])
    y_net = net_income(y)
    vmax = -Inf
    amax = 0.
    for ai_next in eachindex(asset_grid)
        a_next = asset_grid[ai_next]
        # now we include net income in the budget constraint
        # instead of just income
        c = y_net + a - a_next/(1+r)
        if c > 0
            @views v = utility(c, σ) + β * dot(Π[:, yi], V[:, ai_next, t+1])
            if v > vmax
                vmax = v
                amax = a_next
            end
        end
    end
    return vmax, amax
end
```

Now let's consider a couple of different versions of the net income function (these are also in `income_tools.jl`).
```{julia}
#| eval: false
no_tax(x) = x

progressive_tax(x,λ,τ) = λ * x^(1-τ)
```

```{julia}
μ = log(10.) #
egrid,Π = tauchen(5,0.9,0.1)
T = 60
income_grid = [μ+egrid[i] for i in 1:5, t in 1:T]
p = (;
    T,
    asset_grid = LinRange(0,100,100),
    income_grid,
    β = 0.96,
    r = 0.04,
    Π,
    σ = 2.,
    net_income = no_tax
)

```

How could we ensure that the progressive tax is self financing (i.e. obeys the resource constraint)?  For a given value of $\tau$, we can pick $\lambda$ to ensure that the average allocation is equal to average income.

The code below uses `solve_steady_state` from recitation 2 to find the stationary distribution of $\Pi$ and calculates the $\lambda$ that obeys the resource constraint given $\tau$. Note that this code works under two assumptions:

1. $\mu_{t}$ is constant over time $t$; and
2. The initial draw of $y$ is taken from the stationary distribution of $\Pi$, $\pi^*$.

```{julia}
function solve_lambda(τ,ygrid,pi_star)
    return dot(pi_star,ygrid) / dot(pi_star,ygrid.^(1-τ))
end

# choose progressivity
τ = 0.2
# solve for the stationary distribution
pi_star = solve_steady_state(p.Π)
# solve for λ
λ = solve_lambda(τ,exp.(income_grid[:,1]),pi_star)

```

Now we can try solving the model and comparing values with and without this tax system.

```{julia}
p_new = (;p...,
    net_income = x->progressive_tax(x,λ,τ))

model0 = solve_model(p)
model1 = solve_model(p_new)

```

```{julia}
plot(model0.V[:,1,1],label="no taxes")
plot!(model1.V[:,1,1],label = "progressive taxes")
```

Both regimes use the same income grid, so here it is fine to compare the value functions state by state.

# Welfare decompositions in the model

To decompose the average welfare gain into components, let's first calculate the terms we need. Regime $A$ is the economy with no taxes (`model0`) and regime $B$ is the economy with progressive taxes (`model1`).

```{julia}
(;σ,β) = p
# 𝒱(c): value of consuming c for sure in every period
V_cert(x) = (1-β^T)/(1-β) * utility(x,σ)
# certainty equivalents for each initial income state
cbar0 = ((1-σ)*(1-β)/(1-β^T) * model0.V[:,1,1]).^(1/(1-σ))
cbar1 = ((1-σ)*(1-β)/(1-β^T) * model1.V[:,1,1]).^(1/(1-σ))
# average certainty equivalents
Cbar0 = dot(pi_star,cbar0)
Cbar1 = dot(pi_star,cbar1)
# utilitarian welfare
W0 = dot(pi_star,model0.V[:,1,1])
W1 = dot(pi_star,model1.V[:,1,1])

```

And with these in hand we can calculate the decomposition:
```{julia}
ω = (W1/W0)^(1/(1-σ)) - 1
ω_I = Cbar1 / Cbar0 - 1
ω_R = ((W1 / V_cert(Cbar1)) / (W0 / V_cert(Cbar0)))^(1/(1-σ)) - 1

println("Total gain (ω):            ", round(100ω, digits=2), "%")
println("Insurance (ω_I):           ", round(100ω_I, digits=2), "%")
println("Redistribution (ω_R):      ", round(100ω_R, digits=2), "%")
println("Check: (1+ω_I)(1+ω_R) - 1 = ", round(100*((1+ω_I)*(1+ω_R) - 1), digits=2), "%")
```

The output above tells us that introducing progressive taxation is equivalent to raising consumption by $100\times\omega$ percent in all periods and states of the world. Most of this gain comes from improved insurance against income shocks rather than from redistribution.

These steps are packaged into the function `welfare_decomposition` in `income_tools.jl`, which returns the same three numbers:

```{julia}
welfare_decomposition(model0.V[:,1,1], model1.V[:,1,1], pi_star, p)
```

To conclude, let's re-calculate this decomposition for a more persistent value of $\rho$ and interpret the results. As in recitation 2, we hold the unconditional variance of $\varepsilon$ fixed so that we only change persistence, not total risk.

```{julia}
σ_ε = 0.1 / sqrt(1 - 0.9^2)   #<- unconditional SD when ρ = 0.9
ρ = 0.99
egrid,Π = tauchen(5,ρ,σ_ε*sqrt(1-ρ^2))
income_grid = [μ+egrid[i] for i in 1:5, t in 1:T]
p = (;p..., income_grid, Π)

# solve for the stationary distribution
pi_star = solve_steady_state(p.Π)
# solve for λ
λ = solve_lambda(τ,exp.(income_grid[:,1]),pi_star)

p_new = (;p...,
    net_income = x->progressive_tax(x,λ,τ))

model0 = solve_model(p)
model1 = solve_model(p_new)

res = welfare_decomposition(model0.V[:,1,1], model1.V[:,1,1], pi_star, p)
println("Total gain (ω):            ", round(100res.ω, digits=2), "%")
println("Insurance (ω_I):           ", round(100res.ω_I, digits=2), "%")
println("Redistribution (ω_R):      ", round(100res.ω_R, digits=2), "%")
```

Notice that the welfare gains are now coming almost entirely from redistribution and not from insurance. When we look at the transition matrix $\Pi$, we see that to numerical precision, the income shocks are essentially permanent:

```{julia}
Π
```

which explains why the welfare gains derive purely from redistribution: once the initial draw is made, there is (almost) no remaining risk to insure.
